name: Yusuf Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign. Our conversation is confidential, including anything different from your public answer. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Yusuf, 58, and a junior electrician with a vocational certificate. I came into this after the print shop where I worked closed, and I'm still below the experienced crew in practical skill. Today I sorted fittings and helped prepare a cable run under supervision, then had to ask the senior worker to show me a drawing again. I use AI every day to quiz myself on study notes, but recognising the answer on a screen doesn't mean my hands can do the task without checks.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home life like, and what matters to you about change?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner works in an accounts office, and our grown children have homes of their own. We rent, I earn typical trade pay, we've saved three months of normal expenses and there are some similar employers nearby. I enjoy trying a new tool early, but I think workers should have paid learning time and access to proper support rather than face every change alone. I can see retirement as a question ahead, not an income I've verified; old employment records still need checking. For now both wages cover the bills.

say: I'd keep **small useful tools** without asking them to remake the whole world.
I'd retain the **supervisor's checks** and avoid making every evening a race to keep up.
think: Both **household wages** should continue in this mild picture, with three months saved against ordinary interruptions.
Being a **frustrated beginner** doesn't mean my work or living feels insecure when the paid jobs continue.
do: Continue **supervised preparation** and fitting now and through the first plateau year.
Keep the **checked study routine** and household budget, asking before unfamiliar site work rather than buying another course.
feel: **Calm** about household living, with curiosity about gradually improving practical skills.
S0.quote: I can remember words faster than my hands learn a method.
fieldNote: His **calm** follows two covering wages and a moderate reserve, while daily AI study doesn't promote him beyond junior supervised work.
He separates **current security** from unresolved retirement resources, treating no course, new subscription or future exit as already chosen.

steps.text: Continue supervised preparation and fitting with checked study and the normal household budget

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a small tool could help without making a new world out of it. I'd keep the study questions and the supervisor's practical checks. I don't need every evening to become a test of whether I'm keeping up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd expect both household wages to carry on much as now in this picture, with three months saved for an interruption. That makes our living feel secure over the next few years. Being a beginner still frustrates me, but I wouldn't turn that frustration into a claim the wage was disappearing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep the ordinary supervised preparation and fitting work. Through the first plateau year I'd keep the checked study routine and normal household budget, asking the senior worker before using anything unfamiliar on site. I'd buy no new course or subscription just to prove I liked learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about money in that picture, and interested in slowly becoming more useful. I'd enjoy getting one practical task right. I wouldn't need to replace a small success with another announcement to chase.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the study quizzes went better than the practical work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the practical demonstration again rather than let a good quiz result flatter me. I can remember words faster than my hands learn a method. The check belongs to the work, not to my mood about asking for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the reserve settle the retirement question?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd still need the actual income records, living costs and timing before saying we could stop earning. Three months saved is useful but isn't a retirement wage. I'd keep those questions separate from enjoying a steady week.

say: I'd recognise **accounts work** as directly exposed even while much of my own day remains practical.
I'd ask for **paid required learning** while being honest that liking a tool doesn't settle my partner's wage.
think: My partner's **paid hours** could shrink as software takes checking and customer replies.
My practical work may hold longer, but our **three-month reserve** doesn't make a household income cut irrelevant.
do: Learn the **AI audio-note tool** only with written approval, approved software, invented jobs and paid time, retaining normal wages and hours.
Require **supervisor checks** before any draft becomes a work record, keeping practical work supervised.
Review **actual household wages** against essential bills monthly during the first year, assigning no unchosen career to my partner.
feel: **Anxious** about the household wage, while interested in a bounded new tool function.
S1.quote: A useful trial can wait for proper terms.
fieldNote: His **new AI learning** is an audio-note function, separate from existing daily study questions and conditional on written paid-time approval.
The **supervisor's check** precedes record use, while invented examples protect private data and practical electrical responsibility remains beyond the tool.

steps.text: Learn the approved AI audio-note tool with written approval and invented jobs only during paid work
Retain normal wages and hours; require supervisor checks before drafts become work records
Keep practical tasks supervised and review actual household wages against essential bills monthly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the accounts office sounds more directly exposed than my work carrying and fitting things. I'd tell my partner I could enjoy a study tool and still worry about what happened to paid office hours. I'd ask the firm to pay for any learning it required from us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner's hours could shrink as checking and customer replies moved into software. My own practical hours might hold longer, but we'd still feel the household income cut. Three months saved gives us room to ask, not a second wage agreement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask for written employer approval to learn the approved AI audio-note tool on invented job examples during paid work, with normal wages and hours retained. I'd require the supervisor to check every draft before it became a work record. In the first year I'd keep supervised practical tasks and compare actual household wages with bills monthly, without choosing my partner's next career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the household, and still interested in trying a function I hadn't used. I wouldn't be overwhelmed by the tool. I'd be worried about whether the learning time and the other wage remained paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would protect private information in the audio-note trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave real customer details and private conversations out, using only invented examples for the trial. If written approval or protected paid time wasn't there, I wouldn't start it. A useful trial can wait for proper terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would learning the tool change your electrical responsibilities?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it's a way to organise a draft, not proof that I understood the drawing or chose the right fitting. I'd keep the senior worker's practical checks. I wouldn't let a tidy note make me look ready for work I still needed help to do.

I'd seek paid work and **support terms** before treating a possible replacement income as part of the household budget.

My **junior practical hours** face later physical competition, and three months saved may not bridge a dependable new income.
do: Request **association record advice** subject to availability, counting no retirement income or support before verification and approval.
Sign a **shared paid-teaching request** with any fees funded and normal paid hours and wages retained, assuming no agreement.
Keep **suitable supervised work** during 2029 only while available, reviewing actual household wages and essentials monthly.
feel: **Alarmed** about expected major household income loss, with sleep disturbed despite continuing work and practical requests.
S2.quote: A study app can't turn an old employment letter into the next rent payment.
fieldNote: His **household alarm** begins with expected accounts-income loss at the thinking date, before robots reach his own practical work.
He preserves **availability and approval limits** around records and support, while the paid-teaching request becomes neither an agreement nor course enrollment.

steps.text: Request association record advice subject to availability, counting no unverified or unapproved income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking work changes in 2028 when I'd be 60, with capable robots around 2031 when I'd be 63. My partner's accounts work wouldn't get the physical trade's extra years. I'd want paid work and support terms explained before we counted a different income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd expect a large part of the accounts wage to go in 2028, and our usual budget still needs both wages. My junior practical hours could face the later robots too. I'd be awake calculating whether three months of expenses was enough time to find anything dependable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd request help from the workers' association advice service to obtain official retirement records and check actual support eligibility, subject to availability and no payment assumed. I'd sign a shared request for paid practical teaching with any fees funded and normal paid hours and wages retained, without calling it agreed. During 2029 I'd keep suitable supervised paid work while available and compare actual household wages with essentials monthly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about a large household loss, even while I could still work and make the requests. I wouldn't count a possible retirement figure as money that had already arrived. A study app can't turn an old employment letter into the next rent payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the association advice service to verify?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask which official records were needed, what any income could actually be paid from and what conditions applied. We'd check whether proposed support was a grant or loan and what it cost. I'd keep the household budget on confirmed income while the application or terms were unresolved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the paid-teaching request mean a course had started?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want real teaching on tasks I was actually expected to do, with a qualified person checking me. But I haven't enrolled in a course by signing a request for paid learning. I wouldn't spend the reserve to make the request look as if it had already succeeded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years should let us check an actual path rather than make the older worker's birthday into a plan. I'd be 63 at the thinking change in 2031 and about 66 when robots followed around 2034. I'd still ask for paid practical teaching now, while I needed the wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I still expect a large loss of the accounts wage in 2031 without a confirmed replacement, and that keeps me awake. More time gives us a chance to check the official records and actual work, not a wage that's already promised. I can't assume a retirement payment or suitable job at 63 or 66.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd maintain the shared request for paid teaching, funded fees and normal paid hours and wages retained, counting no agreement until written. I'd request association help with official records and eligibility, subject to availability and no income counted before confirmation. During 2032 we'd compare verified income, essential costs and actual suitable work before deciding whether I could stop or still needed wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still alarmed about the expected household gap, with more time to check before a decision. I'd want someone to see that a birthday and a reserve can both be real without producing the missing income. I wouldn't call us ready just because I could fill in the form quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you choose a course or job for your partner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd ask what tasks, fees and paid time were actually offered, but my partner would choose any application. Being good with a tool doesn't make me the planner of someone else's working life. We'd need the real household figures in front of both of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the retirement records were incomplete?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we'd ask the provider or former employer how to obtain the official information and keep the budget on confirmed wages meanwhile. I'd ask for help understanding the reply rather than invent an amount. Missing information isn't a payment I can spend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives us time to find real resources, not permission to ignore the household wage that could change first. I'd be 68 at the thinking change in 2036 and about 71 when robots followed around 2039. I'd still seek paid teaching while I needed work now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner's accounts hours could shrink before the full thinking change, so I'd be anxious about household money over the next few years. Retirement might matter more by 68, but I haven't confirmed an income that replaces the wages. I also can't assume either adult could keep working or find a suitable job then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep suitable supervised paid work while available and the shared request for funded teaching with normal paid hours and wages retained. I'd ask the association service for official-record help, subject to availability, counting no unverified retirement income, support or contribution from the grown children. During 2037 we'd compare confirmed income and costs with actual capacity and suitable work before any decision about stopping or further work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about possible earlier household income loss, though less hurried by the distant robot date. I'd have time to ask twice if a record made no sense. I wouldn't let being quick with a tool hide a question I still needed answered by a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the grown children to contribute?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for help understanding the papers before asking about money. I'd count only help they had chosen and we had agreed, not wages I imagined because they were adults. My grown children's household plans still matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would bring the resource review forward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A wage cut, new essential bill or a change in either person's ability to work. We'd use actual figures straight away rather than wait for 2036. I'd keep any proposal separate from a written agreement or a confirmed payment.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect a large accounts-wage loss before we have another confirmed source, with later risk to my own junior hours. Paid practical teaching with fees covered and wages protected would help, alongside accessible advice on official retirement and support records. A fast answer from a tool doesn't tell me when our next dependable household income starts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether somebody who enjoys learning new tools still needs help with the paper from an old employer. I do. I'd rather admit the missing record than make the household live on my confidence.

headlineQuote: A fast answer from a tool doesn't tell me when our next dependable household income starts.
portrait: **Yusuf, 58**, is a junior electrician with a vocational certificate, below-average practical skill and supervised preparation and fitting tasks.
His **household** has a partner, grown children, rented housing, typical trade pay, three months saved and some nearby electrical employers.
He uses **AI daily for study**, but keeps new tool learning conditional on written approval, paid time, normal wages and supervisor checks.
Expected **accounts-wage losses** alarm him in faster AGI worlds, while retirement resources, support, family contributions and future work capacity remain unverified.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** threatens a large accounts-wage loss before replacement income, with later risk to his own junior hours.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid practical teaching** with fees covered and normal wages protected would make learning affordable.
